Saturday, 15 July, eleven o’clock. The garden of the Fourvière care home. Julien has come alone, as he promised Hélène. She is waiting for him on the bench under the lime tree.
You came. And you came alone. Sit down, Julien. I’m listening.
It was you who asked me to come and tell you in person. So here it is: we’re staying. It’s here that we want to live.
(closes her eyes for a moment) You know, it’s the first time a man has come to tell me he’s staying.
It’s not for your sake that we’re staying, I promise. You had told us not to.
I know. So tell me: what made you decide?
This morning, each of us wrote a word on a piece of paper, without showing the other. Ioana wrote "Lyon". And so did I.
The same words… That’s what a couple is. But Paris was your dream.
It was the dream of a twenty-year-old boy. What I want today is something else. What matters is teaching music to children who have never had access to it.
The director’s project? But you told me it wasn’t certain.
It still isn’t certain. Even if the region says no in December, I’ll start with my pupils, at my school. That’s where you start.
She’s the one signing her letter right now, in Nathalie’s office. From 1 January, her name will be on the door.
(takes his hand) Henri left and never came back to tell me. You stayed, and you came. That’s all I needed.
And now it’s my turn to ask a question. Will you come to Romania in August, for the christening? Ioana’s grandmother is waiting for you for the hora.
(laughs) At eighty-six? That’s madness. (a pause) What time does the plane leave?

In Romanian you highlight something through stress or word order. In French you use a construction: C’EST + the word + QUI + verb, when the word is the SUBJECT:
It was you (and nobody else) who asked me to come.
She’s the one signing her letter.

The verb after "qui" agrees with the pronoun, not with "qui": "C’est moi qui AI une question" (not "qui a"), "C’est nous qui AVONS décidé", "C’est vous qui ÊTES venu". And the pronouns are the stressed ones: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles.
When you highlight a COMPLEMENT (object, place, time, with a preposition), you use C’EST… QUE. The preposition stays in front of the word:
C’est ici que nous voulons vivre.
Nous ne restons pas pour vous.
Ce n’est pas pour vous que nous restons.
C’est de toi que je parle.
In the plural, in careful writing: "Ce sont mes élèves qui…". In speech you often hear "C’est mes élèves qui…".
3. Ce qui…, c’est… / Ce que…, c’est…
The second construction puts the important information at the end, like a little suspense. "Ce qui" is the subject, "ce que" the direct object, "ce dont" replaces "de + something":
What matters is teaching music to children.
What I want today is something else.
The choice works as with relative pronouns (ch. 21 and 39): the verb needs a subject → ce qui; a direct object → ce que; "de" → ce dont.
Au cas où tu aurais faim… / à condition que tu sois…
Bien que ce soit dur… / même si c’est…

On Saturday 15 July, at seven in the morning, neither Ioana nor Julien had really slept. Rose-Hélène, on the other hand, was babbling in her cot, perfectly rested. They sat down at the kitchen table, in front of two cups of tea, like two players before a game of chess.

It was Ioana who had the idea. "When my parents had to make a big decision," she said, "my mother would take two pieces of paper. Each of them wrote a word, without showing it. Then they opened them together. My father says that’s how they chose my name."

Julien smiled. He tore two little squares out of the shopping notebook. They turned their backs to each other, each bent over their paper. Julien hesitated for a long time, pen in the air. Ioana wrote straight away, then folded her paper four times, like a very secret letter.

"On three," said Ioana. "One, two, three." They opened the papers at the same time. On Ioana’s it said "Lyon", in big letters. On Julien’s too: "Lyon". And underneath, smaller, he had added: "with you".

They stayed silent for a while, looking at the two papers. Then Ioana burst out laughing, then she cried, then she laughed again. Julien took her in his arms. In the cot, Rose-Hélène gave a little cry of joy, as if she had understood everything.

"What’s funny," said Julien, "is that I’ve known since Paris. Since the first street corner where I wondered what you would think of it." Ioana wiped her eyes. "And I’ve known since the list. What I’d written at the bottom was already the answer."

At eight, Julien called Olivier Marchand. He had prepared a long speech to apologise, but he didn’t have time to give it. At the very first words, Marchand burst out laughing. "Lyon, is it? I knew it. Don’t apologise. I’ll be the one sending you an email to explain."

Then he called Claire Vasseur. She answered on the first ring, as if she had been waiting by the phone. "It’s in Lyon that I want to start," said Julien. "Even if nothing is signed." There was a silence. Then: "Come on Monday at nine. We have an orchestra to create."

Meanwhile, Ioana had gone to the office. Although it was Saturday, Nathalie was waiting for her, sitting at her big glass desk, the letter in front of her. She didn’t ask anything. She just held out a pen. Ioana signed. Nathalie took a bottle of champagne out of a drawer.

"It’s nine in the morning," Ioana protested. "Exactly," Nathalie replied. "It’s the best time to become a partner." Raising her glass, she asked: "Just tell me one thing. Was it you who chose Lyon, or him?" Ioana smiled. "It was us."

Leaving the office, Ioana stopped in front of the entrance door. The gilded plaque read only "Atelier Rhône". In six months, her name would be engraved there, next to Nathalie’s. She took a photo of the empty plaque and sent it to her mother, without a word. Elena replied with three hearts and a Romanian flag.

At eleven, as he had promised, Julien went up to Fourvière alone to tell Hélène, on the garden bench. He came back down an hour later, his eyes red, holding a little sachet of lavender she had slipped into his pocket. He never told anyone everything they had said to each other.

In the afternoon they told everyone the news. Odile, who had made a cherry clafoutis "in case there was something to celebrate", kissed each of them three times. "It’s the best news of the year," she said. "After the little one’s birth, of course."

Radu, for his part, cried without the slightest shame. He still had yellow paint behind his ears. "If you’d left," he admitted, "I’d have had to learn to cook. Lucia can only make tortillas." Lucia elbowed him, then hugged Ioana very tight.

Karim, on the phone, shouted so loudly that Julien had to hold the phone away from his ear. "I’m the one who told you to go and see the director! You owe me a dinner!" Behind him you could hear Leïla laughing: "Another dinner! With all the bets in this story, the whole of Lyon is going to eat for free."

Pierre and Brigitte, in Annecy, put the phone on speaker so that Manon could hear too. "It’s the best decision you could have made," said Pierre. "Even if, between ourselves, it’s Annecy you should have moved to." Brigitte took the phone out of his hands. "Don’t listen to him. What matters is that you’re happy. And that the little one is two hours from us, not five."

The last to hear the news was Théo. Julien called him at the end of the day. There was a long silence on the line, then a cry of joy, then the voice of his mother, the lady from the town hall, asking what was going on. "It’s my teacher!" Théo yelled. "He’s staying!"

In the evening, Ioana called Iași. Elena and the grandmother appeared on the screen, listening without understanding why Ioana was laughing so much. When she had explained everything, Elena applauded. The grandmother just nodded, as if she had never doubted it. Then she said in Romanian: "Bine. Acum, botezul."

For that was the next adventure: Rose-Hélène’s christening, on 15 August, in the little village church. Everyone wanted to come. Pierre and Brigitte had already booked their tickets, Manon had bought a dress, Karim and Leïla were rehearsing their roles as godfather and godmother.

And above all, Hélène had said yes. The care home doctor had refused at first, then agreed, on condition that she used a wheelchair at the airports and that Odile went with her. Odile had replied that she wouldn’t miss this trip for anything in the world.

That evening, once everyone had gone and the little one was finally asleep, Julien sat down at the piano. He placed the two scores side by side: Henri’s and his own. He had played them dozens of times, but never one after the other.

He began with Henri’s waltz, slow and a little melancholy. Then, on the last note, without stopping, he went straight into his own. And he discovered something incredible: the two waltzes were in the same key. The end of one led naturally into the beginning of the other, as if they had been written to follow each other.

Ioana had fallen asleep on the sofa, her head on a cushion, a smile on her lips. Victor, back via the balcony, was asleep at her feet. Julien played the two waltzes three times in a row, very softly, so as not to wake anyone. A single story, he thought, begun in 1962 and still going on tonight.

Before switching off the light, he took the two little papers from the morning, the ones on which they had written "Lyon", and slipped them into the yellowed envelope, with Henri’s score. One day, on her twentieth birthday, Rose-Hélène would find them. And she would know that it was here that everything had begun, and here that everything had carried on.
